Description: A gentle activity that supports head and neck control.
Why It Matters: In these first months your baby is working on the very first physical task of life: holding their own head steady and learning that their body belongs to them. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Recline on a sofa or propped-up pillows, baby face-down on your bare chest, one hand supporting their back. Get face-to-face: your face is their strongest motivation to lift their head.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; WHO Motor Development; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports head and neck control.
Why It Matters: In these first months your baby is working on the very first physical task of life: holding their own head steady and learning that their body belongs to them. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Lay baby face-down on a firm, clean surface. Place a rolled muslin under chest to ease the lift. Start 2 min and add 1 min per week.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; WHO Motor Development; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building leg strength and kicking.
Why It Matters: Babies this age cannot yet control their movements, so this is about giving the body the right opportunities rather than teaching a skill. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Lay baby on back; hold ankles gently and move legs in slow cycling motions. Say 'pedal, pedal' rhythmically while maintaining eye contact.
Source: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians; IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building head and neck control.
Why It Matters: In these first months your baby is working on the very first physical task of life: holding their own head steady and learning that their body belongs to them. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Gently hold baby's forearms, slowly extend arms outward, then bring hands together at midline over chest. Repeat 5 times each side.
Source: WHO Motor Development Milestones; AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports visual tracking with head movement.
Why It Matters: Every small movement now is building the neck, shoulder and trunk strength that rolling and sitting will later depend on. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Hold a high-contrast B&W card 25 cm from baby's face. Move it slowly left then right. Let eyes find it before you move again.
Source: WHO Motor Development Milestones; AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports early trunk support.
Why It Matters: In these first months your baby is working on the very first physical task of life: holding their own head steady and learning that their body belongs to them. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Hold baby upright against your shoulder and let them practice holding their head for 10–15 seconds. Support gently: don't grip.
Source: WHO Motor Development Milestones; AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports leg strength and kicking.
Why It Matters: In these first months your baby is working on the very first physical task of life: holding their own head steady and learning that their body belongs to them. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Hold a light scarf 15 cm above baby's feet while they lie on back. Let them discover kicking makes it move: first cause-effect feedback.
Source: WHO Motor Development Milestones; AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports early rolling.
Why It Matters: Every small movement now is building the neck, shoulder and trunk strength that rolling and sitting will later depend on. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Place baby on their side with a rolled towel tucked behind their back for support. Alternate sides each session; 5 min per side.
Source: WHO Motor Development Milestones; AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building reflexive grasp.
Why It Matters: Your baby's hands are mostly working on reflex at this stage, and this gently invites them to open, feel and eventually grasp on purpose. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Place your index finger in baby's palm and let the grasp reflex close around it. Gently tug to stimulate the grip.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports reflexive grasp.
Why It Matters: Before a baby can reach for anything they need to discover their hands exist, and this is part of that discovery. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: With warm hands make small circular motions across each palm and each finger. Open fisted hands gently with thumb-stroke wrist to fingertips.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports reflexive grasp.
Why It Matters: Before a baby can reach for anything they need to discover their hands exist, and this is part of that discovery. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: When baby's fists are clenched, gently stroke from wrist to fingertips along the back of the hand to encourage opening.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports reflexive grasp.
Why It Matters: Before a baby can reach for anything they need to discover their hands exist, and this is part of that discovery. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Gently bring baby's hands together at the centre of their chest. Hold 3 seconds, release. This builds bilateral brain coordination.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building reflexive grasp.
Why It Matters: Hand movements are still involuntary now, so this is about sensation and awareness rather than skill. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Hold baby's forearm steady and gently rotate the wrist in small circles, 5 times each direction on each hand.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports reflexive grasp.
Why It Matters: Before a baby can reach for anything they need to discover their hands exist, and this is part of that discovery. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Place a small rolled cloth in baby's palm. Note how long the grasp reflex holds it and whether they bring it toward their mouth.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports early vocal play.
Why It Matters: Long before your baby says a word, they are learning the rhythm, pitch and melody of your language, and that learning happens now. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Talk through every nappy change, feed, and bath. 'Now I'm lifting your legs. This might feel cool.' Tone matters more than words.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep Guidance; IAP; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building rhythm and melody of language.
Why It Matters: Your voice is the most important sound in your baby's world, and every bit of talk builds the foundation for later language. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Sing one consistent song at the same time each day. Repetition builds a neural safety pattern. Same song, same voice, every day.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports early vocal play.
Why It Matters: Babies absorb the patterns of speech months before they can produce any of it, which is why talking to them matters so early. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: When baby makes any vowel sound, mirror it back exactly. Pause 10 full seconds before speaking again: that gap is the lesson.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports early vocal play.
Why It Matters: Long before your baby says a word, they are learning the rhythm, pitch and melody of your language, and that learning happens now. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: After speaking or making a sound, count to 10 silently before responding again. You are teaching conversation structure.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building early vocal play.
Why It Matters: Long before your baby says a word, they are learning the rhythm, pitch and melody of your language, and that learning happens now. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Call baby's name from 1 metre away (not from directly in front). Watch for eyes or head turning toward the sound.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports early vocal play.
Why It Matters: Babies absorb the patterns of speech months before they can produce any of it, which is why talking to them matters so early. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Introduce one new household sound daily: wooden spoon on pot, rustling paper, running water. Watch how baby stills and locates.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports rhythm and melody of language.
Why It Matters: Your voice is the most important sound in your baby's world, and every bit of talk builds the foundation for later language. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Use a slightly higher pitch and slower pace than normal when talking to baby. This is biologically optimal for infant language processing.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports exposure to language patterns.
Why It Matters: Babies absorb the patterns of speech months before they can produce any of it, which is why talking to them matters so early. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Read any book, recipe, or message aloud to baby. The vocabulary range and rhythm matter: comprehension is irrelevant at this stage.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports visual attention and tracking.
Why It Matters: Newborn vision and attention are still developing, and this gives them exactly the kind of input that helps them along. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Hold a black-and-white card 25 cm from baby's face. Let them fixate 10 seconds before moving slowly left. Newborn vision peaks at this distance.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child; Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports face recognition.
Why It Matters: Your baby's brain is building its very first expectations about the world, mostly through what they see and hear repeatedly. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Hold your face 20–30 cm from baby's. Make one slow exaggerated expression and hold it. Wait 10 seconds for their response.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child; Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports visual attention and tracking.
Why It Matters: At this stage thinking looks like looking: attention, recognition and noticing what is familiar. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Hold a small unbreakable mirror 25 cm from baby. They won't recognise themselves yet, but the responsive face is deeply engaging.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports face recognition.
Why It Matters: Your baby's brain is building its very first expectations about the world, mostly through what they see and hear repeatedly. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Cover your face with your hands. Hold 3 seconds. Reveal warmly. Very early object permanence and social anticipation practice.
Source: Piagetian developmental framework; Harvard Center on the Developing Child; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building visual attention and tracking.
Why It Matters: Newborn vision and attention are still developing, and this gives them exactly the kind of input that helps them along. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Carry baby toward a window or lamp. Let them observe light change as you move closer and further. Narrate: 'Bright! Now darker.'
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child; Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building visual attention and tracking.
Why It Matters: Newborn vision and attention are still developing, and this gives them exactly the kind of input that helps them along. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Hold a high-contrast picture book 25 cm from baby. Spend 20–30 seconds on each page before turning. One page can hold attention this age.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child; Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building comfort and co-regulation.
Why It Matters: Your baby cannot calm themselves yet, so being soothed by you is how their nervous system learns what calm feels like. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Undress baby to nappy and hold against bare chest tummy-to-tummy. Cover both lightly. Regulates temperature, cortisol, and heart rate.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep Guidance; IAP; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports early social connection.
Why It Matters: This is the beginning of the relationship, and at this age closeness and responsiveness are the whole task. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: When baby makes a mouth movement or social smile, reflect it back immediately and wait. You are teaching: my expression has social power.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Attachment); Zero to Three; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building comfort and co-regulation.
Why It Matters: This is the beginning of the relationship, and at this age closeness and responsiveness are the whole task. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: When baby cries, respond before escalation. Consistent early response builds the secure attachment base for all future relationships.
Source: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians; IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports comfort and co-regulation.
Why It Matters: Your baby cannot calm themselves yet, so being soothed by you is how their nervous system learns what calm feels like. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Name what you see: 'You look uncomfortable. Let me see what's wrong.' Labelling emotional states builds the circuits for self-regulation later.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Attachment); Zero to Three; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports comfort and co-regulation.
Why It Matters: Your baby cannot calm themselves yet, so being soothed by you is how their nervous system learns what calm feels like. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Let each main caregiver hold baby skin-to-skin. Each person's unique warmth and heartbeat is a distinct and valuable regulatory experience.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Attachment); Zero to Three; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports comfort and co-regulation.
Why It Matters: Your baby cannot calm themselves yet, so being soothed by you is how their nervous system learns what calm feels like. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: When you feel anxious, slow your own breathing while holding baby. They sense and entrain to your nervous system state.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Attachment); Zero to Three; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building tactile input and body awareness.
Why It Matters: Sensory experience is how a newborn learns about their own body and the world around it. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Warm oil in palms. Begin with legs: least sensitive. Long slow strokes hip to foot, then arms, back, head. Stimulates vagus nerve.
Source: AYUSH Ministry guidance on infant massage; IAP; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports tactile input and body awareness.
Why It Matters: Your baby's nervous system is learning to make sense of touch, sound and movement, and gentle input helps it organise. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Gently touch different textures to baby's palm and feet: soft cloth, smooth wood, cool spoon. Name each: 'Soft. Smooth. Cool.'
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports visual processing.
Why It Matters: Sensory experience is how a newborn learns about their own body and the world around it. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Take baby outside for 10–15 min. Wind, natural light, birdsong, and temperature variation are multi-sensory inputs no indoor space can replicate.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building visual processing.
Why It Matters: Sensory experience is how a newborn learns about their own body and the world around it. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: During bath, with baby always within arm's reach, pour water at slightly different temperatures on hands. Narrate: 'Warm water now. A little cooler.' Never leave baby unattended in water, even briefly.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building auditory processing.
Why It Matters: Sensory experience is how a newborn learns about their own body and the world around it. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Place baby against your chest and hum or sing. The physical vibration is felt across their whole body and is deeply calming.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building feeding rhythm and hunger cues.
Why It Matters: Daily care routines are your baby's first experience of predictability, and predictability is what makes them feel safe. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Learn early hunger cues: rooting, hand-to-mouth, stirring. Feed before crying. Responding to early cues builds baby's signal-response trust.
Source: IAP Infant Care Guidance; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building sleep and wake rhythms.
Why It Matters: At this age self-care is entirely done for your baby, and the value lies in how calm and consistent it feels. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Track awake time: 0–6 weeks = 45–60 min; 6–12 weeks = 60–90 min. Beginning sleep routine before overtiredness sets in improves settling.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep Guidance; IAP; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports head and neck control.
Why It Matters: Every small movement now is building the neck, shoulder and trunk strength that rolling and sitting will later depend on. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Place an interesting toy just out of reach during tummy time. The motivation to lift and reach makes effort more sustained.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; WHO Motor Development; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building head and neck control.
Why It Matters: In these first months your baby is working on the very first physical task of life: holding their own head steady and learning that their body belongs to them. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: In tummy time, gently rock baby's hips toward one side. Give the nervous system the sensation of weight transfer needed for rolling.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; WHO Motor Development; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports early rolling.
Why It Matters: Babies this age cannot yet control their movements, so this is about giving the body the right opportunities rather than teaching a skill. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Place baby on their back. Gently cross one leg over the other and let momentum encourage rolling to the side. Celebrate any attempt.
Source: WHO Motor Development Milestones; AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building early trunk support.
Why It Matters: Every small movement now is building the neck, shoulder and trunk strength that rolling and sitting will later depend on. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Sit baby on your lap facing outward, hands loosely around their trunk. Let them feel the work: don't over-support.
Source: WHO Motor Development Milestones; AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports head and neck control.
Why It Matters: Babies this age cannot yet control their movements, so this is about giving the body the right opportunities rather than teaching a skill. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: In tummy time, once baby pushes up on forearms, gently rock their hips side to side. This is the direct predecessor of rolling.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; WHO Motor Development; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports leg strength and kicking.
Why It Matters: Babies this age cannot yet control their movements, so this is about giving the body the right opportunities rather than teaching a skill. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Hold your palms against baby's feet while they lie on back. Let them push: this activates leg extensors used later for standing.
Source: WHO Motor Development Milestones; AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building leg strength and kicking.
Why It Matters: In these first months your baby is working on the very first physical task of life: holding their own head steady and learning that their body belongs to them. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Hold baby upright on your lap, supporting under arms, and let them bounce slightly. Vestibular input and leg strength combined.
Source: WHO Motor Development Milestones; AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports head and neck control.
Why It Matters: Babies this age cannot yet control their movements, so this is about giving the body the right opportunities rather than teaching a skill. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Prop an unbreakable mirror in front of baby during tummy time. Their own face is one of the strongest motivators to lift the head.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep and Tummy Time; WHO Motor Development; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building hand awareness and early grasp.
Why It Matters: Your baby's hands are mostly working on reflex at this stage, and this gently invites them to open, feel and eventually grasp on purpose. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Hang a lightweight object (cloth, spoon) just above baby's chest while they lie on back. Wait: let them discover swiping makes it move.
Materials Required: Cloth, ribbon, or spoon on string
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports reflexive grasp.
Why It Matters: Before a baby can reach for anything they need to discover their hands exist, and this is part of that discovery. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Offer a toy wider than one hand. Watch whether they use both hands together: bilateral integration milestone appearing around 4–5 months.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building reflexive grasp.
Why It Matters: Your baby's hands are mostly working on reflex at this stage, and this gently invites them to open, feel and eventually grasp on purpose. At this age your only job is to offer it warmly and let your baby respond however they do; there is nothing to achieve and nothing to get right.
How To Do It: Give a toy in one hand, then offer a second near the other. Do they transfer the first, or hold both? Transfer appears around 5–6 months.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports hand awareness and early grasp.
Why It Matters: Hand movements are still involuntary now, so this is about sensation and awareness rather than skill. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Hand baby a small sealed container (lid glued or taped shut) with dried lentils inside. Let them discover shaking makes sound: first voluntary cause-effect action. Never use an unsealed container with loose lentils at this age.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports hand awareness and early grasp.
Why It Matters: Hand movements are still involuntary now, so this is about sensation and awareness rather than skill. Keep it short and stop as soon as your baby looks away or fusses. Their attention span is measured in moments, and that is normal.
How To Do It: Give a piece of crinkled paper or foil (supervised). The sound, texture, and visual feedback engage three senses simultaneously.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building hand awareness and opening.

How To Do It: Press a textured surface gently against baby's palm: a mesh bag, rough towel, smooth cup. The hand's sensory map is being built now.
Source: AOTA Early Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports early vocal play.

How To Do It: When baby coos or babbles, echo it back exactly. Then add one new syllable: 'ooh… and then… ba?' Pause 10 seconds each time.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A simple everyday moment that supports early vocal play.
Why It Matters: Your voice is the most important sound in your baby's world, and every bit of talk builds the foundation for later language. Repetition matters far more than variety now, so the same thing tomorrow is exactly right.
How To Do It: Try raspberry sounds, sudden peekaboo, lifting gently in the air. The belly laugh (appearing around 3–4 months) is a major milestone.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports listening and early vocal play.

How To Do It: Model ba-ba-ba, ma-ma-ma, da-da-da during alert windows. These are the first consonants baby will produce at 5–6 months.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A gentle activity that supports listening and voice recognition.

How To Do It: Speak in two languages fluidly during routines. 'Now we're washing your hands: haath dho rahe hain.' Bilingual input from birth is a gift.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building response to voice.

How To Do It: Point to each family member and say their name slowly. 'This is Dadi. Dadi.' Repetition over weeks builds face-name recognition.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building early vocal play.

How To Do It: Play a different musical genre each day this week: classical, folk, jazz, film songs. Varied sound builds auditory discrimination.
Source: WHO Screen Time Guidelines (under 5); IAP Screen Time Guidance; IAP

Description: A calm, close activity for building response to voice.
