How To Do It: Ask baby to carry a small bag with a few books inside across the room. Heavy carrying is regulating to the sensory system.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops first mark-making.
Why It Matters: This is the age where hands become genuinely useful tools, and that happens through hundreds of small attempts. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Show drawing a horizontal line across paper and let baby try. Any deliberate directional mark is an achievement.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for rotational hand control.
Why It Matters: This is the age where hands become genuinely useful tools, and that happens through hundreds of small attempts. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Practice opening and closing containers with twist lids. Rotation movements are a distinct fine motor skill used in daily life.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for stacking and controlled release.
Why It Matters: This is the age where hands become genuinely useful tools, and that happens through hundreds of small attempts. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: 6-block tower requires spatial planning, grip calibration, and controlled release. Each additional block is harder than it looks.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds bilateral tearing.
Why It Matters: Small hands need a great deal of repetition, and this builds the strength and control that self-feeding and dressing will require. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Provide magazines or old newspaper for tearing. Bilateral tearing requires both hands working in opposition: a coordination milestone.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds threading and hand-eye coordination.
Why It Matters: This is the age where hands become genuinely useful tools, and that happens through hundreds of small attempts. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Thread 5 large beads or pasta pieces onto a shoelace, with close, constant supervision: beads should never be left within reach when unsupervised. Requires visual targeting, bilateral coordination, and sustained attention.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops hand strength and early dexterity.
Why It Matters: This is the age where hands become genuinely useful tools, and that happens through hundreds of small attempts. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: A simple inset puzzle builds visual discrimination, spatial rotation, and the tolerance for trial-and-error failure.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first words and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Vocabulary at this age grows through repeated, everyday exchanges far more than through teaching. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: By 18 months, 20–50 words (including approximations) is the developmental target. Under 10 words by 18 months warrants a paediatrician mention.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first words and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Vocabulary at this age grows through repeated, everyday exchanges far more than through teaching. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: More doodh', 'bye dada', 'big ball.' Two-word phrases by 18 months are a major milestone. Model them in all conversation.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first words and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Your toddler understands much more than they can say, and this closes that gap. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Baby will point at everything and say 'woh kya hai?' or similar. Every time: name it, describe it in one sentence, wait.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds early narrative and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Your toddler understands much more than they can say, and this closes that gap. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Tell a simple 3-sentence story about something that happened today. Story structure (beginning, middle, end) is absorbed before it is produced.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops first words and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Vocabulary at this age grows through repeated, everyday exchanges far more than through teaching. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Kutte kya bolta hai? Bhow bhow!' Sound-to-animal linking builds vocabulary through a different encoding channel.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first words and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: First words appear in this window, and they appear faster in children who are talked with rather than talked at. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Focus on verbs this week: running, eating, sleeping, jumping. Action vocabulary is as important as noun vocabulary.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep Guidance; IAP; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops early narrative and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Your toddler understands much more than they can say, and this closes that gap. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Same book, multiple days in a row. When baby anticipates a page, they are demonstrating memory, sequence, and language: simultaneously.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops first words and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: First words appear in this window, and they appear faster in children who are talked with rather than talked at. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: In familiar songs, pause on the last word of each line and wait. By 18 months many babies fill in the word: word retrieval practice.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for imitation and early pretend play.
Why It Matters: Toddlers learn by trying things and seeing what happens, and this gives them something worth investigating. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Give baby pots, spoons, and empty containers. Let them 'cook.' Pretend play now represents real sequences observed in daily life.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds early sorting and matching.
Why It Matters: This builds early problem-solving at an age when persistence is short and everything is experimental. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Sort objects into two groups by shape: round things here, flat things there. Demonstrate; don't expect immediate success.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops object permanence and searching.
Why It Matters: Toddlers learn by trying things and seeing what happens, and this gives them something worth investigating. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Show a picture of a cup, then ask baby to find the real cup. Picture-object correspondence is an abstract cognitive skill.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds early memory.
Why It Matters: This builds early problem-solving at an age when persistence is short and everything is experimental. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Begin a familiar routine and stop mid-way. Watch baby signal or try to complete it: sequence memory is confirming itself.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops number word awareness.
Why It Matters: Toddlers learn by trying things and seeing what happens, and this gives them something worth investigating. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Place 1, then 2, then 3 objects in a line counting aloud as you do. One-to-one correspondence is being seeded; production comes later.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops simple problem-solving.
Why It Matters: Understanding at this stage is built through direct experience, repeated many times. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Tape a desirable toy lightly to a table or box. Watch how baby figures out removing the tape or pulling the object free.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops emotional vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Emotional skills at this age are learned by being helped through feelings, over and over. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: When emotions arise, sit close and name the emotion specifically: 'You're angry. That felt unfair.' Don't fix: just name and stay.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops emotional vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is discovering they are a separate person with their own wants, which is why this stage is intense. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Put a simple 4-face chart on the wall: happy, sad, angry, scared. 'How are you feeling today? Point to the face.' No judgment.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for separation tolerance.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is discovering they are a separate person with their own wants, which is why this stage is intense. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Develop a 3-step goodbye sequence for separations. Consistent, brief, warm: never long and uncertain. Consistency reduces distress.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first turn-taking.
Why It Matters: Emotional skills at this age are learned by being helped through feelings, over and over. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Sit facing each other and roll a ball back and forth. Taking turns in a structured physical game is cooperative play emerging.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops emotional expression and early social skills.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is discovering they are a separate person with their own wants, which is why this stage is intense. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: When a character in a book is sad or scared, narrate: 'Woh dara hua hai. Tum kya sochte ho?' Perspective-taking through story.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds wanting to contribute.
Why It Matters: Emotional skills at this age are learned by being helped through feelings, over and over. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Let baby 'help' wipe a surface, stir food, hand you objects. Social participation and competence are both being built.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for tactile exploration.
Why It Matters: Messy, tactile play at this age builds tolerance that makes eating and dressing easier too. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: This month use a different fill each week: sand, water, dried beans, shredded paper. Sensory tolerance broadens with variety.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops tactile exploration.
Why It Matters: Toddlers need a lot of sensory input, and providing it deliberately often reduces the seeking behaviour that looks like mischief. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Walking barefoot on grass, sand, or dirt provides proprioceptive richness that shoes remove. 10 minutes barefoot outdoors = rich input.

Description: An everyday activity that develops tactile exploration.

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for auditory processing.

How To Do It: Make the same sound loudly and quietly: the same instrument or voice. Can baby identify louder and quieter? Auditory discrimination.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds vestibular (balance) input.
Why It Matters: Messy, tactile play at this age builds tolerance that makes eating and dressing easier too. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Roll baby gently in a blanket: not tight. The whole-body deep pressure is calming for the nervous system and delights most toddlers.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds self-feeding with a spoon.
Why It Matters: Skills like these take far longer when a toddler does them, and that time is the investment. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Offer fork for stabbing soft foods. Fork + spoon both available. Child chooses: autonomy in eating builds a positive food relationship.
Source: IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; AAP Toilet Training Guidance; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for hygiene routines.
Why It Matters: Skills like these take far longer when a toddler does them, and that time is the investment. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Demonstrate hand washing before every meal and after outdoors. By 18 months, with reminding and help, this is beginning to establish.

Description: An everyday activity that develops early running.

Description: A simple activity that builds early jumping.

Description: A simple activity that builds climbing and stepping coordination.

Description: A simple activity that builds standing balance.

Description: A simple activity that builds climbing and stepping coordination.

Description: An everyday activity that develops early throwing and ball skills.

Description: An everyday activity that develops walking and dynamic balance.

Description: An everyday activity that develops first mark-making.

How To Do It: Show drawing a circle slowly and let toddler try. Circle before straight lines: fine motor milestone at 24–27 months when it appears.

Description: A simple activity that builds stacking and controlled release.

Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for bilateral tearing.

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for hand strength.

Description: A simple activity that builds threading and hand-eye coordination.

Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first words and vocabulary.

How To Do It: When toddler asks 'why' (it starts!), answer simply and then ask 'why do you think?' Turn every why into a conversation.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds early narrative and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Vocabulary at this age grows through repeated, everyday exchanges far more than through teaching. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: After reading a familiar book, close it and ask 'What happened?' Listen for any sequence: even one event recalled is narrative memory.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first words and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: First words appear in this window, and they appear faster in children who are talked with rather than talked at. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Introduce one colour per week. Label it consistently all week: 'The red cup. Your red shoes. Red tomatoes!' One at a time works best.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops following simple instructions.
Why It Matters: Vocabulary at this age grows through repeated, everyday exchanges far more than through teaching. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Pick up the cup AND bring it to me.' Two unrelated steps in sequence tests working memory as well as language.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops first words and understanding.
Why It Matters: Vocabulary at this age grows through repeated, everyday exchanges far more than through teaching. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Ask open questions about recent experiences: 'What did you see at the park?' Don't correct answers: expand and continue.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds cause-and-effect reasoning.
Why It Matters: Understanding at this stage is built through direct experience, repeated many times. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Stack 3 books then push: watch toddler's face. Set up a ramp and roll a ball down. Multi-step cause-effect chains are interesting now.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for early sorting and matching.
Why It Matters: Understanding at this stage is built through direct experience, repeated many times. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Use pictures or objects: sort animals from foods. Categorisation by function or type is a major cognitive leap.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds early problem-solving and matching.
Why It Matters: Understanding at this stage is built through direct experience, repeated many times. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: After a routine, ask what comes next: 'We had bath. Then what? Then what?' Three-event sequence recall is emerging.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds shape and spatial matching.
Why It Matters: Understanding at this stage is built through direct experience, repeated many times. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: 6–8 piece puzzle requiring rotation and trial-and-error. The frustration tolerance needed here is as developmental as the spatial skill.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds number word awareness.
Why It Matters: Understanding at this stage is built through direct experience, repeated many times. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Place 3 objects in a line and count them together: touch each as you count. One-to-one correspondence beginning to appear.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops early sorting and matching.
Why It Matters: Toddlers learn by trying things and seeing what happens, and this gives them something worth investigating. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: 4 pairs of matching cards face-down. Turn over 2 at a time. Early working memory and concentration.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops early emotional regulation.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is discovering they are a separate person with their own wants, which is why this stage is intense. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Before a frustrating task, name the strategy: 'If this is hard, take a breath.' Practice during calm so it is available during frustration.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops first turn-taking.
Why It Matters: Emotional skills at this age are learned by being helped through feelings, over and over. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Establish clear turn-taking in a simple game. 'Meri baari. Ab tumhari baari.' Consistent language makes the rule learnable.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops emotional expression and early social skills.
Why It Matters: Emotional skills at this age are learned by being helped through feelings, over and over. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Point out someone who is sad or hurt. 'Woh roh raha hai. Use dard hua. Hum kya kar sakte hain?' Empathy is taught through narration.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for emotional expression and early social skills.
Why It Matters: Emotional skills at this age are learned by being helped through feelings, over and over. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Set up a tea party or cooking scenario with dolls. Taking roles in pretend play is social cognition and narrative combined.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for emotional vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Emotional skills at this age are learned by being helped through feelings, over and over. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: When toddler is upset, model the phrase: 'I don't like that' or 'Mujhe yeh pasand nahi.' Give them words for their feelings.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds early emotional regulation.
Why It Matters: Emotional skills at this age are learned by being helped through feelings, over and over. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Introduce a simple self-comfort strategy in a calm moment: slow breathing, squeezing a soft object. Practice before it is needed.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops water play and sensory regulation.
Why It Matters: This supports the sensory processing that underlies calm, settled behaviour. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Two containers of water, a cup for transferring. Supervised water play for 15 min. Pouring, splashing, and measuring emerge naturally.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops tactile exploration.
Why It Matters: Messy, tactile play at this age builds tolerance that makes eating and dressing easier too. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: With an adult handing over and collecting the knife each time, roll, flatten, and cut atta dough with a blunt knife. Making shapes adds visual-motor control to the tactile input.
Source: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians; IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops tactile exploration.
Why It Matters: Toddlers need a lot of sensory input, and providing it deliberately often reduces the seeking behaviour that looks like mischief. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Walk outside and collect one of each: a leaf, a stone, a stick, a feather. Touch and describe each one together.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds sensory exploration and tolerance.
Why It Matters: Messy, tactile play at this age builds tolerance that makes eating and dressing easier too. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Blow bubbles and let toddler pop them. Tracking, reaching, timing, and the satisfying pop make this multi-sensory and motivating.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for tolerating messy textures.
Why It Matters: Toddlers need a lot of sensory input, and providing it deliberately often reduces the seeking behaviour that looks like mischief. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Finger painting (food-safe paint or safe craft paint). Each colour is introduced separately. Direct contact with material.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for beginning to dress.
Why It Matters: Toddlers want to do things themselves, and channelling that into real self-care tasks works with the drive rather than against it. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Name each clothing item as it goes on. Ask toddler to help push arm through sleeve or lift foot for shoe. Participation builds independence.
Source: IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; AAP Toilet Training Guidance; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops hygiene routines.
Why It Matters: This builds genuine independence at an age when wanting to be independent is at its peak. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Brush teeth together at the same time. Letting toddler hold and attempt the brush first builds cooperation with the hygiene routine.
Source: IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; AAP Toilet Training Guidance; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds early running.
Why It Matters: Toddlers need to move a great deal, and this gives that energy somewhere useful to go while building balance and strength. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Set up household obstacles to run around: chairs, cushions, a line of tape. Navigating while running requires real-time motor planning.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops early jumping.
Why It Matters: Toddlers need to move a great deal, and this gives that energy somewhere useful to go while building balance and strength. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Put a tape line on the floor. Jump over with both feet. Clearing an obstacle while jumping = significantly harder than jumping in place.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for walking and dynamic balance.
Why It Matters: Toddlers need to move a great deal, and this gives that energy somewhere useful to go while building balance and strength. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Practice walking backward, first holding hands then free. Backward locomotion requires body-awareness and spatial recalibration.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds early throwing and ball skills.
Why It Matters: At this age balance is still developing, and each attempt refines it a little further. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Roll a large ball back and forth, then graduate to low throwing and catching. Catching a rolling ball before a thrown one.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops walking and dynamic balance.
Why It Matters: Walking is new and still effortful, so this kind of practice is what turns a wobbly skill into an automatic one. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Practice on a tricycle or balance bike. Pedalling requires reciprocal leg movement: the same pattern as walking but with sustained force.
Source: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians; IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for walking and dynamic balance.
Why It Matters: Toddlers need to move a great deal, and this gives that energy somewhere useful to go while building balance and strength. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Demonstrate a gallop (lead-foot, drag) and encourage copying. Galloping before skipping: the intermediate coordination step.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds walking and dynamic balance.
Why It Matters: Toddlers need to move a great deal, and this gives that energy somewhere useful to go while building balance and strength. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Encourage alternating feet on the way up the stairs. May still need rail; alternating feet up is a 24–30 month milestone.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds functional strength and carrying.
Why It Matters: Toddlers need to move a great deal, and this gives that energy somewhere useful to go while building balance and strength. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Encourage pushing a chair or pulling a loaded bag. Resistance exercise builds core strength and spatial navigation simultaneously.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for first mark-making.
Why It Matters: Small hands need a great deal of repetition, and this builds the strength and control that self-feeding and dressing will require. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Show a horizontal line (left to right) and ask child to copy. Directionality in drawing precedes directionality in writing.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for first mark-making.
Why It Matters: Fine motor skill at this stage is built through play rather than practice, and this offers plenty of both. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Demonstrate a circle slowly and let child try. Circle-copying typically appears 24–30 months: earlier than + or V shapes.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for bilateral tearing.
Why It Matters: This is the age where hands become genuinely useful tools, and that happens through hundreds of small attempts. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: With an adult supervising closely, use child-safe scissors to snip fringe into paper strips. Each snip is a complete bilateral motor action.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for pouring and wrist control.
Why It Matters: Small hands need a great deal of repetition, and this builds the strength and control that self-feeding and dressing will require. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Pour water from a small jug into a cup. The control of flow is a daily self-care fine motor skill used for years.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for hand strength and early dexterity.
Why It Matters: This is the age where hands become genuinely useful tools, and that happens through hundreds of small attempts. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: 8–10 piece puzzle requiring rotation and spatial reasoning. Systematically trying each piece before accepting failure is the cognitive goal.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops grasp-and-release control.
Why It Matters: Small hands need a great deal of repetition, and this builds the strength and control that self-feeding and dressing will require. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Sort household objects into 3 colour groups. Naming the colours correctly while sorting combines language and cognition.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; AAP Developmental Milestones; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for first words and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: First words appear in this window, and they appear faster in children who are talked with rather than talked at. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: 200 words by 24 months is the benchmark (CDC). Under 50 words by 24 months is worth professional discussion.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first words and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Your toddler understands much more than they can say, and this closes that gap. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Mama, more water please.' Three-word phrases mark a significant vocabulary and grammar step appearing 21–24 months.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops first words and understanding.
Why It Matters: Vocabulary at this age grows through repeated, everyday exchanges far more than through teaching. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: I want' and 'Give me' appearing means self-concept is strongly established. Model these forms throughout the day.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first words and understanding.
Why It Matters: First words appear in this window, and they appear faster in children who are talked with rather than talked at. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: What happened at the park today?' Not 'Did you have fun?' Open questions require memory, sequencing, and language simultaneously.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for early narrative and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: First words appear in this window, and they appear faster in children who are talked with rather than talked at. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: During book reading, stop before a page turn: 'What do you think will happen next?' Prediction requires language plus narrative cognition.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops first words and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Your toddler understands much more than they can say, and this closes that gap. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Not a colour worksheet: just naming colours of real objects throughout the day. Context makes the association stronger.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds early narrative and vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Your toddler understands much more than they can say, and this closes that gap. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Cat (bat) sat: mat!' Rhyming awareness at 24 months predicts reading readiness. Even partial awareness is worth celebrating.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first words and understanding.
Why It Matters: First words appear in this window, and they appear faster in children who are talked with rather than talked at. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: At bedtime, ask child to tell you two things that happened today. This builds narrative language and episodic memory together.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep Guidance; IAP; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for early sorting and matching.
Why It Matters: Toddlers learn by trying things and seeing what happens, and this gives them something worth investigating. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Sort objects into two groups: big and small. Size concept develops through sorting, not worksheets.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for early problem-solving and matching.
Why It Matters: Toddlers learn by trying things and seeing what happens, and this gives them something worth investigating. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Ask: 'What do we do after breakfast? Then what?' Three to four event sequence recall is the target at this age.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops shape and spatial matching.
Why It Matters: Toddlers learn by trying things and seeing what happens, and this gives them something worth investigating. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Build a simple colour or shape pattern: red, blue, red, blue, and leave a gap. Can child predict what comes next?
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for early problem-solving and matching.
Why It Matters: This builds early problem-solving at an age when persistence is short and everything is experimental. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Pour water into an empty glass; let child pour it back. 'Full. Empty. Full again.' Concrete object manipulation precedes abstract concept.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds object permanence and searching.
Why It Matters: This builds early problem-solving at an age when persistence is short and everything is experimental. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Show baby photos of family members. Can child identify who it is? Memory across time = abstract object permanence.
Source: Piagetian developmental framework; Harvard Center on the Developing Child; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds number word awareness.
Why It Matters: Understanding at this stage is built through direct experience, repeated many times. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Place 4 objects in a line; touch each as you count 1-2-3-4. Guide child's hand to touch each. Counting with meaning, not reciting.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); Zero to Three; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds playing near other children.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is discovering they are a separate person with their own wants, which is why this stage is intense. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: During play: 'You have 4 blocks. Can you give me 2?' Guided sharing builds number concept alongside social skill.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds first turn-taking.
Why It Matters: Emotional skills at this age are learned by being helped through feelings, over and over. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Build something together: 'I put one block, you put one block.' Turn-taking in construction is cooperative play at its clearest.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Serve and Return); IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops emotional vocabulary.
Why It Matters: Emotional skills at this age are learned by being helped through feelings, over and over. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Name 5 emotions accurately this week: happy, sad, angry, scared, excited. Emotional vocabulary directly predicts social competence.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for emotional expression and early social skills.
Why It Matters: Toddlers have very big feelings and almost no ability to manage them, so this is about support rather than teaching. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Join child's pretend play and add a new element: 'The baby is sleeping: shall we sing her a lori?' Extending the narrative.
Source: AAP Safe Sleep Guidance; IAP; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops early emotional regulation.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is discovering they are a separate person with their own wants, which is why this stage is intense. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Teach a specific phrase for frustration: 'I need help' or 'Mujhe madad chahiye.' Practice during calm: not during the moment.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for emotional expression and early social skills.
Why It Matters: Toddlers have very big feelings and almost no ability to manage them, so this is about support rather than teaching. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: When child hurts or upsets another: 'What could you say? How do you think they felt?' Modelling, not forcing. Empathy precedes apology.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; UNICEF Responsive Caregiving; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds tactile exploration.
Why It Matters: This supports the sensory processing that underlies calm, settled behaviour. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Walk barefoot on grass, sand, and smooth pavement on the same outing. Noticing the difference is the sensory lesson.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A simple activity that builds water play and sensory regulation.
Why It Matters: Toddlers need a lot of sensory input, and providing it deliberately often reduces the seeking behaviour that looks like mischief. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Add food colouring to water in clear cups and mix two together. Watching red + blue = purple is both science and sensory.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: An everyday activity that develops auditory processing.
Why It Matters: This supports the sensory processing that underlies calm, settled behaviour. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: Pots, boxes, metal bowls: each makes a different sound. Let child experiment with what each material produces.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for tactile exploration.
Why It Matters: Messy, tactile play at this age builds tolerance that makes eating and dressing easier too. Follow their interest rather than the instructions, and stop while they are still enjoying it.
How To Do It: Press small objects into dough to make impressions. Roll thin snakes. With an adult handing over and collecting the knife each time, cut with a blunt knife. Precision work in tactile medium.
Materials Required: Atta dough and objects to press
Source: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians; IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for sensory exploration and tolerance.
Why It Matters: This supports the sensory processing that underlies calm, settled behaviour. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: Wrap child in a heavy blanket on a lap. Deep pressure input is calming for the autonomic nervous system.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for beginning to dress.
Why It Matters: This builds genuine independence at an age when wanting to be independent is at its peak. Expect them to want it again immediately, and again after that; repetition is how toddlers learn.
How To Do It: By 24 months: pull trousers up and down, remove shoes and socks, help with shirts. All with support: independence is incremental.
Source: IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; AAP Toilet Training Guidance; IAP

Description: A playful, repeatable activity for toilet training readiness.
Why It Matters: This builds genuine independence at an age when wanting to be independent is at its peak. Let your toddler lead where possible, and accept that it will be slower and messier than doing it yourself.
How To Do It: If interest appears: describe what toilet training involves. Let child see the process. No pressure: readiness signs should lead.
Source: IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; AAP Toilet Training Guidance; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing jumping and explosive leg power.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is becoming genuinely capable physically, and this builds the strength and coordination that running, climbing and jumping all need. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Encourage jumping forward from standing, landing on both feet. Distance of jump increases each week as leg strength grows.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing static and dynamic balance.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is becoming genuinely capable physically, and this builds the strength and coordination that running, climbing and jumping all need. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: A plank, a garden wall, or tape on the floor. Walk along without falling off. Balance on a narrow path is a 2.5-year skill.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing jumping and explosive leg power.
Why It Matters: This is a good age for challenging the balance system, because the body is stable enough to try and still learning fast. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Hold child's hand and encourage hopping on one foot. Even one hop is the milestone beginning: don't expect sustained hopping yet.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: An activity that builds throwing, catching and hand-eye coordination.
Why It Matters: This is a good age for challenging the balance system, because the body is stable enough to try and still learning fast. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Bounce a large ball to child. Catching a bounced ball before a thrown one: the visual tracking time is longer.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing pedalling and steering.
Why It Matters: Movement at this age is how the body's control systems get calibrated, and children who move more move better. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Tricycle: practice steering around objects. Combining pedalling with directional control is a significant motor coordination step.
Source: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians; IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens jumping and explosive leg power.
Why It Matters: This is a good age for challenging the balance system, because the body is stable enough to try and still learning fast. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Move like different animals: frog jump, bear walk, crab walk, snake slither. Each uses different muscle groups and movement patterns.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: An activity that builds running and speed control.
Why It Matters: This is a good age for challenging the balance system, because the body is stable enough to try and still learning fast. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Demonstrate an overhand throw and let child try. Overhand requires trunk rotation: a very different movement than underhand.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: An activity that builds functional strength and carrying.
Why It Matters: This is a good age for challenging the balance system, because the body is stable enough to try and still learning fast. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Help child do a forward roll on a soft surface. Head tuck, push-off, and landing = vestibular, motor, and spatial all together.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: An activity that builds pre-writing control.
Why It Matters: This strengthens the small muscles of the hand, which matters long before a pencil is ever picked up seriously. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: Show a + (cross) and let child try. Requires two directional lines crossing: harder than circle; appears around 30–36 months.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: An activity that builds hand control and dexterity.
Why It Matters: Hand control is sharpening quickly now, and this builds toward the precision that drawing, cutting and dressing need. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: Fork for stabbing soft foods. The grip and stabbing force are different from a spoon: a distinct fine motor skill.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens rotational and fastening control.
Why It Matters: Your toddler's hands can now do far more than a year ago, and this stretches that capability a little further. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Button, zip, and dress a doll. This is fine motor practice that feels purposeful and maintains engagement longer.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens spatial placement.
Why It Matters: This strengthens the small muscles of the hand, which matters long before a pencil is ever picked up seriously. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Show folding a piece of paper in half and ask child to try. Aligning edges before folding requires spatial and motor precision.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens bilateral coordination and spatial precision.
Why It Matters: Hand control is sharpening quickly now, and this builds toward the precision that drawing, cutting and dressing need. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: Sort blocks by BOTH colour AND size together. Multi-attribute sorting is more demanding than single-attribute.
Materials Required: Blocks in multiple colours and sizes
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens threading and hand-eye coordination.
Why It Matters: Your toddler's hands can now do far more than a year ago, and this stretches that capability a little further. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Lace thread through holes to form a simple picture. Requires planning the sequence of holes to achieve the intended shape.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens sentence building.
Why It Matters: This is a period of rapid vocabulary growth, and conversation is what fuels it. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Ask child to tell a story about an animal they know. Even 2–3 sentences with a character is the emergence of narrative.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens asking and answering questions.
Why It Matters: This is a period of rapid vocabulary growth, and conversation is what fuels it. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Why does it rain?' 'What would happen if…?' Complex question forms are emerging: answer simply and turn it back.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens sentence building.
Why It Matters: Sentences are forming now, and children build them by hearing slightly more complex language than they can produce. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Consistent 3–4 word sentences with grammar: 'I want the red ball.' Grammar errors ('I goed') are developmentally correct now.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens asking and answering questions.
Why It Matters: Sentences are forming now, and children build them by hearing slightly more complex language than they can produce. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Does cat rhyme with bat? What about cat and dog?' Detecting rhyme before producing it: typical at 25–30 months.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens sentence building.
Why It Matters: Language at this age develops through back-and-forth exchanges, where your toddler gets a real turn. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: Show a picture and ask 'What is happening here?' Child describes scene: vocabulary, grammar, and observation all combined.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: An activity that builds asking and answering questions.
Why It Matters: This is a period of rapid vocabulary growth, and conversation is what fuels it. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Practice saying full name. 'What is your full name?' is a social comprehension milestone by age 3.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing asking and answering questions.
Why It Matters: This is a period of rapid vocabulary growth, and conversation is what fuels it. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Have a 5-turn conversation where child asks at least one question. Asking is more advanced than answering.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: An activity that builds asking and answering questions.
Why It Matters: Sentences are forming now, and children build them by hearing slightly more complex language than they can produce. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: After reading a favourite book many times, ask child to 'read' it to you from the pictures. Memory narrative is emerging.
Source: ASHA Speech and Language Milestones; AIISH India language norms; IAP

Description: An activity that builds early number sense.
Why It Matters: Sorting, counting and matching all begin here, and they begin through play rather than instruction. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: Place up to 5 objects in a line and count together, touching each one. One-to-one correspondence solidifying now.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); NAEYC Play-Based Learning; IAP

Description: An activity that builds comparing attributes.
Why It Matters: This is the age where children start to reason about why things happen, not just notice that they do. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Big/small, hot/cold, fast/slow, loud/quiet. Opposites build comparative conceptual thinking.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); NAEYC Play-Based Learning; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing problem-solving and early concepts.
Why It Matters: This is the age where children start to reason about why things happen, not just notice that they do. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Yesterday we went to the park. Today we are home.' Time concepts past/present solidify through consistent narration.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); NAEYC Play-Based Learning; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens sorting and categorising.
Why It Matters: Your toddler can now hold an idea in mind and work toward it, which makes this kind of thinking activity genuinely useful. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: Sort objects into 4 groups: food, animals, clothes, vehicles. Four-category sorting is sophisticated categorical thinking.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); NAEYC Play-Based Learning; IAP

Description: An activity that builds working memory.
Why It Matters: Your toddler can now hold an idea in mind and work toward it, which makes this kind of thinking activity genuinely useful. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: Build red-blue-red-blue and leave a gap: 'What comes next?' Pattern extension requires holding the rule in working memory.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); NAEYC Play-Based Learning; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens early number sense.
Why It Matters: Sorting, counting and matching all begin here, and they begin through play rather than instruction. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Here are 2 bananas. I add 1 more. How many now?' Concrete addition before abstract number.
Source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child (Executive Function); NAEYC Play-Based Learning; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing cooperative play.
Why It Matters: Regulation at this age still depends heavily on a calm adult nearby, and that is exactly as it should be. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: If an imaginary friend appears, engage with them: 'What is their name?' Imaginary companions support language, emotional, and social development.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; IAP

Description: An activity that builds emotional regulation and social play.
Why It Matters: Regulation at this age still depends heavily on a calm adult nearby, and that is exactly as it should be. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: When a conflict arises over a toy: 'What could you offer them to trade?' Negotiation is a social skill that must be taught explicitly.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; IAP

Description: An activity that builds emotional vocabulary and awareness.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is starting to notice other people's feelings, which is the beginning of empathy. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Create a display of child's achievements (drawings, photos). 'You did all of these!' Pride in accomplishment is a social-emotional milestone.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens understanding limits.
Why It Matters: This builds the emotional vocabulary and self-control that make the preschool years easier. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Set up a role-play scenario with simple props. Role-play at 25–30 months involves taking on another's perspective.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens emotional regulation.
Why It Matters: This builds the emotional vocabulary and self-control that make the preschool years easier. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: When feelings escalate, say 'Let's take a pause' and model slow breathing together. Practice before it is needed.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing emotional regulation and social play.
Why It Matters: This builds the emotional vocabulary and self-control that make the preschool years easier. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: While reading or in real life: 'How do you think she felt when that happened?' Perspective-taking practice.
Source: Zero to Three; CASEL Social-Emotional Framework; IAP

Description: An activity that builds tactile discrimination.
Why It Matters: Rich sensory experience at this stage feeds language too, because it gives children something worth describing. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: Tear and paste coloured tissue paper onto card. Tearing texture, paper texture, and glue texture are layered sensory inputs.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens water play and sensory regulation.
Why It Matters: Sensory play remains genuinely developmental at this age, supporting both regulation and fine motor skill. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Watering can, puddles, or garden tap. Child-directed water exploration is rich sensory and cause-effect play.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens tactile discrimination.
Why It Matters: This helps your toddler's nervous system distinguish between different sensations, which supports focus and calm. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Gather 8 objects of varied texture. Sort into 'rough' and 'smooth.' Tactile discrimination is now a language + sensory task.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing vestibular and proprioceptive input.
Why It Matters: Rich sensory experience at this stage feeds language too, because it gives children something worth describing. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: Carrying loaded backpack, pushing a box of books, pulling a weighted trolley. Heavy work regulates the nervous system.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: An activity that builds vestibular and proprioceptive input.
Why It Matters: Rich sensory experience at this stage feeds language too, because it gives children something worth describing. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Spin with arms out, stop, try to stay balanced. Vestibular system input: intentional dizziness and recovery is regulating.
Source: AOTA Sensory Integration; Ayres Sensory Integration framework; IAP

Description: An activity that builds hygiene routines.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is now capable of real independence in daily routines, and doing so builds confidence as much as skill. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Let child brush their own teeth first, then parent finishes. Agency in the sequence builds cooperation with the hygiene routine.
Source: AAP Toilet Training Guidance; AOTA Activities of Daily Living; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens toilet independence.
Why It Matters: This reduces the daily friction of routines by giving your child a genuine role in them. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: If signs of readiness present (knowing when wet, interest in toilet), begin with simple potty introduction. Never forced.
Source: AAP Toilet Training Guidance; AOTA Activities of Daily Living; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens jumping and explosive leg power.
Why It Matters: Movement at this age is how the body's control systems get calibrated, and children who move more move better. Let them repeat it as often as they want, and let them change the rules; both are signs it is doing its job.
How To Do It: From one hop, build to 3–5 consecutive hops on the same foot. Each hop requires rebalancing: rapid balance adjustment developing.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens whole-body strength and coordination.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is becoming genuinely capable physically, and this builds the strength and coordination that running, climbing and jumping all need. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Most children gallop at 2.5 years and skip at 3.5. Practice gallop leading with each foot as the precursor.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing throwing, catching and hand-eye coordination.
Why It Matters: Your toddler is becoming genuinely capable physically, and this builds the strength and coordination that running, climbing and jumping all need. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Graduate from bounced to thrown ball catching. Tracking the trajectory and adjusting arms = complex visual-motor planning.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens pedalling and steering.
Why It Matters: This is a good age for challenging the balance system, because the body is stable enough to try and still learning fast. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: On a tricycle: practice pedalling and stopping at a marked line. Braking intentionally requires coordinated leg action.
Source: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians; IAP Infant and Young Child Feeding; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing climbing and stepping coordination.
Why It Matters: Movement at this age is how the body's control systems get calibrated, and children who move more move better. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Staying close enough to spot and catch if needed, climb a ladder alternating hands and feet: the most complex locomotion pattern children this age attempt.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing jumping and explosive leg power.
Why It Matters: This is a good age for challenging the balance system, because the body is stable enough to try and still learning fast. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Standing close beside, ready to catch, let your child jump off a 30-cm step with both feet landing together. Judging safe heights and landing = spatial and motor cognition combined.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing static and dynamic balance.
Why It Matters: Movement at this age is how the body's control systems get calibrated, and children who move more move better. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: With you standing right beside them ready to steady them, walk a balance beam (tape line) with eyes closed for 2 steps. Eyes-closed balance challenges the proprioceptive system intensely.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: An activity that builds whole-body strength and coordination.
Why It Matters: This is a good age for challenging the balance system, because the body is stable enough to try and still learning fast. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Chase game where child must dodge around obstacles. Reactive motor planning: responding to unexpected changes in a path.
Source: WHO Physical Activity Guidelines (under 5); AAP Physical Activity; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens pre-writing control.
Why It Matters: Your toddler's hands can now do far more than a year ago, and this stretches that capability a little further. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Show a V and ask child to copy. Angular shapes (V, then +, then triangle) appear in sequence after circle.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens pre-writing control.
Why It Matters: Your toddler's hands can now do far more than a year ago, and this stretches that capability a little further. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Ask child to draw a person. Head + one other body part by 30 months = fine motor and representational thinking combined.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: An activity that builds pre-writing control.
Why It Matters: Your toddler's hands can now do far more than a year ago, and this stretches that capability a little further. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Cut along a straight line drawn on paper. Staying on the line requires visual monitoring while maintaining bilateral grip.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing threading and hand-eye coordination.
Why It Matters: Hand control is sharpening quickly now, and this builds toward the precision that drawing, cutting and dressing need. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Peel self-adhesive stickers and place on a target. Two-stage finger action requiring precise coordination.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens bilateral coordination and spatial precision.
Why It Matters: Hand control is sharpening quickly now, and this builds toward the precision that drawing, cutting and dressing need. Praise the effort and the trying rather than the result, especially when it does not go well.
How To Do It: Demonstrate placing a block across two towers and ask child to build the same. Copying spatial models = architecture thinking.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: A playful challenge that strengthens pincer grasp and tool use.
Why It Matters: Your toddler's hands can now do far more than a year ago, and this stretches that capability a little further. Give your toddler time to work it out before stepping in, because the working out is where the learning happens.
How To Do It: Small beads on a thin lace. Fine pincer control plus visual targeting plus threading = high-demand fine motor task.
Source: AOTA Fine Motor Development; Handwriting Without Tears readiness framework; IAP

Description: A hands-on activity for developing sentence building.
